title: IL-5, Thrombopoietin and What a Count Cannot Show
summary: Learn the cytokines that drive eosinophils (IL-5, with IL-3 and GM-CSF) and megakaryocytes (thrombopoietin), how the platelet count feeds back on TPO, why Charcot-Leyden crystals mark eosinophil-rich inflammation rather than allergy alone, and why a normal platelet count does not prove normal megakaryopoiesis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 32 Hit 12 (IL-5 as the key eosinophil growth factor, with GM-CSF and IL-3; major basic protein and helminths), Hit 13 (TPO as the primary regulator of platelet production; supporting cytokines), Trap 5 (eosinophilia with Charcot-Leyden crystals) and Trap 6 (normal platelet count does not prove normal megakaryopoiesis). Checked against Rosenberg 2013, Roufosse 2018, Limaye 1990 (abstract), Su 2018, Thomsen 2023, Kaushansky 2024, Hitchcock 2021, Feng 2015 and Acha 2022. Qualifications: MBP is toxic to helminth larvae in vitro, but Rosenberg 2013 calls the in vivo role of eosinophils in mouse helminth models unclear and controversial; Charcot-Leyden crystals (galectin-10, also in basophils) are reported in asthma, allergic fungal sinusitis and allergic rhinitis as well as helminth lesions; plasma TPO is “usually” inversely proportional to platelet count and the sensing mechanism is debated (sponge and hepatic Ashwell-Morell models). Not taught (pending): Hit 13 platelet lifespan 8–11 days and the 2/3 circulating, 1/3 splenic split (Aster 1966 is a scanned page-image article with no readable text here); IL-3 and kit ligand as megakaryocyte support factors; Trap 6 “giant platelets” and the MPN half of the dodge. Not covered: Number Vault eosinophil half-life figures.

objectives: Name the cytokines that drive eosinophil production and explain why IL-5 is the key one.
Describe how thrombopoietin regulates platelet production and how the platelet count feeds back on TPO.
Interpret Charcot-Leyden crystals and a normal platelet count without over-reading either.

scenes.title: Two reassuring guesses
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two marrow-and-smear puzzles. (1) A traveller just back from the tropics has blood eosinophilia, and Charcot-Leyden crystals are seen in a specimen; a note says “just allergy?”. (2) An older adult with macrocytic anaemia has a normal platelet count; a note says “so the megakaryocytes must be fine?”. Question token: “What is really driving each line?”

cues.text: Two quick guesses reach the bench. A traveller back from the tropics has eosinophilia, and Charcot-Leyden crystals turn up. Someone writes: just allergy.
An older adult has macrocytic anaemia but a normal platelet count. Someone writes: so the megakaryocytes must be fine.
To judge both guesses, look at the signals that drive eosinophils and platelets, and at what the marrow itself shows.

props.label: What is really driving each line?

scenes.title: One signal per line
scenes.altText: Schematic: two marrow production lines. Eosinophil line: progenitors respond to IL-5, IL-3 and GM-CSF; IL-5 has the central role in development, activation and survival; its receptor pairs a specific IL-5Rα chain (eosinophils, basophils, mast cells) with a β chain shared with IL-3 and GM-CSF; IL-5 comes mainly from T helper 2 cells. Platelet line: thrombopoietin (TPO), made mainly in the liver, binds its receptor MPL; it is the most potent stimulator of megakaryocyte progenitors and also supports stem cells; IL-6 and IL-11 only modestly raise platelet production and are not needed for baseline output.

cues.text: Eosinophils grow in the marrow from progenitors that respond to three cytokines: interleukin 5, interleukin 3 and GM-CSF. Of these, IL-5 has the central role in development, activation and survival.
Its receptor has a chain specific to IL-5, found on eosinophils, basophils and mast cells, plus a signalling chain shared with IL-3 and GM-CSF. IL-5 is made mainly by T helper 2 cells.

For platelets, the main signal is thrombopoietin, TPO, made mainly in the liver. It binds the MPL receptor and is the strongest known stimulus for megakaryocyte progenitors. It also supports stem cells.
Other cytokines play a smaller part. Interleukin 6 and interleukin 11 can raise platelet production only modestly, and removing them does not change baseline platelet output.

props.title: Eosinophil line
lines: IL-5Rα + shared β chain · from Th2

scenes.title: How the platelet count talks back
scenes.altText: Schematic feedback loop: liver releases TPO → marrow megakaryocytes → platelets. Model 1 (“sponge”): MPL on platelets binds circulating TPO, which is internalised and degraded, so more platelets leave less free TPO. Model 2: aged, desialylated platelets bind Ashwell-Morell receptors on hepatocytes and switch on TPO gene transcription through JAK/STAT signalling. Summary card: plasma TPO is usually inversely related to platelet count; exactly how the liver senses platelets is still debated. Knockout card: mice lacking Mpl have only about 5–10% of normal megakaryocytes and platelets; in humans, loss of TPO or MPL causes amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia and later aplastic anaemia.

cues.text: TPO output is tied to the platelets themselves. In the sponge model, MPL receptors on platelets bind circulating TPO, then take it in and destroy it. More platelets leave less free TPO.
A newer model adds the liver. Old platelets lose sialic acid from their surface, bind Ashwell-Morell receptors on liver cells, and switch on TPO gene transcription.
So plasma TPO usually runs opposite to the platelet count. But exactly how the liver senses platelets is still debated, so treat this as a usual pattern, not a fixed law.

Without the TPO signal, the line nearly stops. Mice lacking the receptor have only five to ten percent of normal megakaryocytes and platelets, and children lacking TPO or MPL develop amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia and then aplastic anaemia.

scenes.title: What the slide can show
scenes.altText: Left card: eosinophil granules hold major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil cationic protein, eosinophil peroxidase and eosinophil-derived neurotoxin; Charcot-Leyden crystal protein is galectin-10, which crystallises where activated eosinophils gather (basophils carry it too). Crystals have been reported in helminth lesions and also in asthma sputum, allergic fungal sinusitis and allergic rhinitis. Eosinophilia is more often infection in tropical areas and inflammation in industrialised regions. Right card: dysmegakaryopoiesis = micromegakaryocytes, hypolobated or non-lobed nuclei, multiple widely separated nuclei; MDS with isolated del(5q) typically has a normal to raised platelet count with hypolobulated megakaryocytes. Bottom card: hook answers.

cues.text: Eosinophil granules hold toxic cationic proteins, including major basic protein. Charcot-Leyden crystals are crystallised galectin-10, formed where activated eosinophils gather. Basophils carry the protein too.

The crystals have been found in helminth lesions, but also in asthma sputum, allergic fungal sinusitis and allergic rhinitis. They mark eosinophil-rich inflammation, not one cause. And eosinophilia is more often infection in the tropics, inflammation in industrialised regions.

On the platelet side, dysplastic megakaryocytes include micromegakaryocytes, nuclei with too few lobes, and multiple separated nuclei. In myelodysplasia with isolated deletion 5q, the platelet count is typically normal or raised, with hypolobulated megakaryocytes.
Back to the hook. The traveller needs a search for helminths as well as allergy. The normal platelet count does not clear the megakaryocytes: only the marrow can show dysplasia.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Charcot-Leyden crystals = allergy” (✓ they mark eosinophil-rich inflammation of many causes, helminths included); “Normal platelet count = normal megakaryopoiesis” (✓ del(5q) myelodysplasia keeps a normal or raised count with dysplastic megakaryocytes); “Major basic protein proves eosinophils clear worms” (✓ MBP is toxic to larvae in vitro, but the in vivo role of eosinophils in mouse helminth models is unclear).

cues.text: Trap one: Charcot-Leyden crystals mean allergy. No: they mark eosinophil-rich inflammation from many causes, and helminths are one of them.
Trap two: a normal platelet count means normal megakaryocytes. No: myelodysplasia with deletion 5q often keeps a normal or raised count with dysplastic megakaryocytes.
Trap three: major basic protein proves eosinophils clear worms. Careful: it kills larvae in the dish, but in mouse infections the eosinophil role is still unclear.

scenes.title: Five for eos, sponge for platelets
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “IL-FIVE feeds the eosinophils; platelets are a SPONGE for TPO: the more sponge, the less free TPO.” Tokens: IL-5 → eosinophils · TPO → megakaryocytes · platelets soak up TPO. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: IL-five feeds the eosinophils, and platelets are a sponge for TPO. The more sponge, the less free TPO left to drive the marrow.

Where it breaks: IL-3 and GM-CSF also support eosinophils, and some tissue eosinophils survive without IL-5. The liver also senses old platelets, the inverse link is only usual, and a count never shows marrow morphology.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “IL-5 drives eosinophils · Charcot-Leyden crystals = eosinophil-rich inflammation, helminths included”, “TPO drives megakaryocytes · usually opposite to platelet count · normal count ≠ normal marrow”.

cues.text: Interleukin 5 drives eosinophils and thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes, but Charcot-Leyden crystals mark eosinophil-rich inflammation of many causes, helminths included, and a normal platelet count cannot show that the megakaryocytes are normal.

props.label: IL-5 → eosinophils · crystals = eosinophil inflammation, worms too
TPO → megakaryocytes · normal count ≠ normal marrow

explanation.what: Plain language: each blood cell line has a main “grow” signal. Eosinophils listen mostly to IL-5; megakaryocytes, which make platelets, listen mostly to thrombopoietin from the liver. Platelets mop up thrombopoietin, so when platelets are plentiful less of the signal is free. Crystals made from an eosinophil protein point to eosinophil-rich inflammation of many causes, and a platelet count says nothing about what the megakaryocytes look like. Scientific terms: interleukin-5 (IL-5), IL-5 receptor α chain and shared β chain, IL-3, GM-CSF, T helper 2 (Th2) cells, major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), galectin-10 / Charcot-Leyden crystal (CLC) protein, thrombopoietin (TPO), MPL receptor, Ashwell-Morell receptor, desialylation, dysmegakaryopoiesis, micromegakaryocyte, MDS with isolated del(5q).
explanation.why: IL-5 has a central role in eosinophil development, activation and survival, and helminth-infected patients’ cells make selectively more IL-5. TPO is the most potent stimulator of megakaryocyte progenitors; MPL on platelets binds and degrades TPO, and aged desialylated platelets signal the liver to transcribe more TPO, so plasma TPO usually runs opposite to the platelet count. Morphological dysplasia is a property of marrow cells, which a count cannot reveal.
explanation.measure: Eosinophil granules: MBP, ECP, eosinophil peroxidase, eosinophil-derived neurotoxin; CLCs are crystallised galectin-10. Dysmegakaryopoiesis (WHO 2008, as cited by Feng 2015): micromegakaryocytes, hypolobated or non-lobed nuclei, multiple widely separated nuclei. MDS with isolated del(5q): macrocytic anaemia, normal or raised platelet count, hypolobulated megakaryocytes. Mpl-null mice: about 5–10% of normal megakaryocytes and platelets.
explanation.differs: IL-5 (eosinophil-specific α chain) vs IL-3 and GM-CSF (shared β chain, many cell types); TPO (primary platelet regulator) vs IL-6 and IL-11 (modest boost, not needed for baseline); sponge model vs hepatic Ashwell-Morell model; CLCs (eosinophil-rich inflammation) vs a specific diagnosis; platelet count (quantity) vs megakaryocyte morphology (quality).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match a growth factor to its lineage, predict how TPO changes with the platelet count, interpret Charcot-Leyden crystals in a returned traveller, or recognise that del(5q) myelodysplasia can show a normal or high platelet count.

mnemonic.text: IL-FIVE feeds the eosinophils; platelets are a SPONGE for TPO: the more sponge, the less free TPO.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each lineage to its main growth factor and recalls the platelet feedback on TPO.
mnemonic.limitation: IL-3 and GM-CSF also support eosinophils and some tissue eosinophils survive without IL-5; the liver also senses old platelets through the Ashwell-Morell receptor; the inverse TPO–platelet link is only usual and its sensing mechanism is debated; a count never shows marrow morphology.

analogyLimitations: Production lines and feedback loops are schematic.
The sponge picture leaves out hepatic sensing of aged platelets.
takeaway: Interleukin 5 drives eosinophils and thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes, but Charcot-Leyden crystals mark eosinophil-rich inflammation of many causes, helminths included, and a normal platelet count cannot show that the megakaryocytes are normal.

questions.stem: Which pairing of hematopoietic growth factor and the lineage it mainly drives is correct?

options.rationale: Correct. IL-5 has a central role in eosinophil development, activation and survival, with IL-3 and GM-CSF also contributing.
Incorrect. Thrombopoietin is the primary regulator of platelet production; G-CSF is the neutrophil growth factor.
Incorrect. G-CSF drives neutrophils; platelets depend mainly on thrombopoietin.
Incorrect. IL-7 is a growth factor for B and T lymphocytes.

questions.stem: An older adult has macrocytic anaemia and a platelet count of 420 × 10⁹/L. The marrow shows hypolobulated megakaryocytes and an isolated del(5q). Which statement is best supported?

options.text: A normal or raised platelet count is typical of this myelodysplasia and does not exclude dysplastic megakaryocytes
options.rationale: Correct. MDS with isolated del(5q) is characterised by macrocytic anaemia, a normal to elevated platelet count and hypolobulated megakaryocytes.

options.text: Megakaryopoiesis must be normal because the platelet count is not low
options.rationale: Incorrect. A count measures quantity; dysplasia is a morphological finding that only the marrow shows.

options.text: Hypolobulated megakaryocytes are a normal finding at this age
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hypolobated or non-lobed nuclei are part of the definition of dysmegakaryopoiesis.

options.text: The raised count proves the patient lacks thrombopoietin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Loss of thrombopoietin or its receptor causes severe thrombocytopenia, not a raised count.

questions.stem: A traveller returning from the tropics has blood eosinophilia, and Charcot-Leyden crystals are seen in a specimen. What is the best interpretation of the crystals?

options.text: They mark eosinophil-rich inflammation, so helminth infection should be considered alongside allergy
options.rationale: Correct. The crystals are galectin-10 from activated eosinophils; they occur in helminth lesions as well as allergic disease, and eosinophilia in tropical settings is more often infectious.

options.text: They prove the eosinophilia is allergic
options.rationale: Incorrect. The crystals are also reported in helminth lesions, fungal disease and tumours; they do not name a cause.

options.text: They are bacterial crystals indicating contamination
options.rationale: Incorrect. They are a crystallised human protein, galectin-10, found in eosinophils and basophils.
Incorrect. The crystal protein comes from eosinophils and basophils, not platelets.

references.citation: Rosenberg HF, Dyer KD, Foster PS. Eosinophils: changing perspectives in health and disease. Nat Rev Immunol. 2013;13(1):9-22. doi:10.1038/nri3341
references.usedFor: Eosinophils develop in marrow in response to IL-5, IL-3 and GM-CSF; IL-5 central to development, activation and survival; IL-5 from Th2 cells; granule proteins MBP, ECP, eosinophil peroxidase, EDN; Charcot-Leyden crystal protein (galectin-10); MBP and ECP toxic to S. mansoni larvae in vitro, but the role of eosinophils in mouse helminth models is unclear and controversial (eosinophil depletion prolonged larval survival in Strongyloides and Angiostrongylus models).

references.citation: Roufosse F. Targeting the Interleukin-5 Pathway for Treatment of Eosinophilic Conditions Other than Asthma. Front Med (Lausanne). 2018;5:49. doi:10.3389/fmed.2018.00049
references.usedFor: IL-5Rα expressed only by eosinophils, basophils and mast cells; common β chain shared with IL-3 and GM-CSF; IL-5 central but neither entirely necessary nor sufficient (lung-resident eosinophils survive independently of IL-5; IL-3/GM-CSF support survival); patients on anti-IL-5 who travel to helminth-endemic areas should be followed carefully.

references.citation: Limaye AP, Abrams JS, Silver JE, Ottesen EA, Nutman TB. Regulation of parasite-induced eosinophilia: selectively increased interleukin 5 production in helminth-infected patients. J Exp Med. 1990;172(1):399-402. doi:10.1084/jem.172.1.399
references.usedFor: Abstract only (Europe PMC record; the full-text XML held only the reference list): IL-3 and GM-CSF production similar, IL-5 markedly greater in patients with helminth-induced eosinophilia.

references.citation: Su J. A Brief History of Charcot-Leyden Crystal Protein/Galectin-10 Research. Molecules. 2018;23(11):2931. doi:10.3390/molecules23112931
references.usedFor: CLC protein/galectin-10 overexpressed in eosinophils, also in basophils and macrophages; CLCs form where eosinophils cluster; reported in helminth lesions (pork tapeworm, filarial worms), hepatic aspirates with helminth infection, allergic fungal sinusitis, asthma sputum, allergic rhinitis, tumours and leukaemia.

references.citation: Thomsen GN, Christoffersen MN, Lindegaard HM, et al. The multidisciplinary approach to eosinophilia. Front Oncol. 2023;13:1193730. doi:10.3389/fonc.2023.1193730
references.usedFor: Eosinophilia more likely due to infection in tropical areas and inflammation in industrialised regions; secreted galectin-10 precipitates as Charcot-Leyden crystal protein indicative of eosinophil activity; eosinophils contribute to control of helminth infections.

references.citation: Kaushansky K. Thrombopoietin, the Primary Regulator of Platelet Production: From Mythos to Logos, a Thirty-Year Journey. Biomolecules. 2024;14(4):489. doi:10.3390/biom14040489
references.usedFor: TPO as primary regulator of platelet production; most potent megakaryocyte colony-stimulating factor; supports HSC survival and, with SCF, expansion; IL-6 or IL-11 modestly (about 50%) stimulate platelet production but their deletion does not alter baseline; lineage growth factors (G-CSF neutrophils, IL-5 eosinophils, IL-7 lymphocytes); human TPO or c-Mpl loss causes amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia and aplastic anaemia.

references.citation: Hitchcock IS, Hafer M, Sangkhae V, Tucker JA. The thrombopoietin receptor: revisiting the master regulator of platelet production. Platelets. 2021;32(6):770-778. doi:10.1080/09537104.2021.1925102
references.usedFor: TPO and MPL as primary regulators of platelet production; TPO mainly produced in the liver; plasma TPO usually inversely proportional to platelet count, sensing mechanisms controversial; platelet sponge model; desialylated platelets and hepatic Ashwell-Morell receptors increasing THPO transcription via JAK/STAT; Mpl-null mice ~5–10% megakaryocytes and platelets.

references.citation: Feng G, Gale RP, Cui W, et al. A systematic classification of megakaryocytic dysplasia and its impact on prognosis for patients with myelodysplastic syndromes. Exp Hematol Oncol. 2015;5:12. doi:10.1186/s40164-016-0041-6
references.usedFor: WHO 2008 definition of dysmegakaryopoiesis (micromegakaryocytes, hypo-lobed or non-lobed nuclei, multiple widely separated nuclei); no precise WHO definition of micromegakaryocyte; across MDS, more micromegakaryocytes associated with lower platelet counts; del(5q) associated with hypo-lobed and un-lobed megakaryocytes. Europe PMC lists the year as 2015 although the volume is 5.

references.citation: Acha P, Mallo M, Solé F. Myelodysplastic Syndromes with Isolated del(5q): Value of Molecular Alterations for Diagnostic and Prognostic Assessment. Cancers (Basel). 2022;14(22):5531. doi:10.3390/cancers14225531
references.usedFor: 5q- syndrome / MDS with isolated del(5q): macrocytic anaemia, normal to elevated platelet count, hypolobulated megakaryocytes; JAK2 V617F in about 6% of MDS-5q, associated with higher platelet counts.

claims.text: Eosinophils develop in response to IL-5, IL-3 and GM-CSF; IL-5 central; receptor chains; Th2 source; selectively increased IL-5 in helminth infection.
Granule proteins; MBP/ECP toxic to helminth larvae in vitro, in vivo role of eosinophils in mouse helminth models unclear.
CLCs are galectin-10 crystals from eosinophils (also basophils); reported in helminth lesions and in allergic and fungal disease; eosinophilia more often infectious in the tropics.
TPO is the primary regulator of platelet production, mainly hepatic, acts via MPL, potent megakaryocyte progenitor stimulator and HSC support; IL-6/IL-11 modest; knockout and human loss phenotypes.
Plasma TPO usually inversely proportional to platelet count; sponge and Ashwell-Morell models; sensing debated.
Dysmegakaryopoiesis features; MDS with isolated del(5q) has normal or raised platelets with hypolobulated megakaryocytes.
G-CSF drives neutrophils; IL-7 drives B and T lymphocytes (question distractors).

Platelet lifespan 8–11 days; 2/3 circulating and 1/3 splenic; IL-3 and kit ligand as megakaryocyte support factors; giant platelets with micromegakaryocytes in MPN/MDS despite a normal count; eosinophil half-life figures.
claims.note: Not taught as facts. Aster 1966 (J Clin Invest 45:645-657) is available only as page images, so its splenic pooling data were not read.

claims.text: “IL-five feeds the eosinophils; platelets are a sponge for TPO.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 32 Hit 12 says eosinophils kill helminths via major basic protein. Rosenberg 2013 reports MBP and ECP are toxic to schistosome larvae in vitro but calls the role of eosinophils in mouse helminth models unclear and controversial; the lesson teaches the in vitro toxicity and the uncertainty (register flag rv-ch32-mbp-helminth-uncertain).

Ch. 32 Trap 5 dodge (“think helminths, not just hay fever”) is sound but incomplete: Su 2018 reports Charcot-Leyden crystals (galectin-10, also in basophils) in helminth lesions and also in asthma, allergic fungal sinusitis, allergic rhinitis and tumours, so they mark eosinophil-rich inflammation rather than any one cause (register flag rv-ch32-clc-nonspecific).

Ch. 32 Trap 6 states TPO is inversely proportional to platelet mass. Hitchcock 2021 says plasma TPO is usually inversely proportional to platelet count and the sensing mechanism is controversial (platelet sponge plus hepatic Ashwell-Morell signalling). The trap’s “giant platelets” and MPN examples were not verified; the lesson uses MDS with isolated del(5q) (normal or raised count, hypolobulated megakaryocytes; Acha 2022) and notes that across MDS more micromegakaryocytes go with lower counts (Feng 2015) (register flag rv-ch32-tpo-inverse-context).

morphology.note: No micrographs; cells, crystals and megakaryocytes are described on cards only.

verification.notes: All 7 taught factual claims checked against open sources (Rosenberg 2013, Roufosse 2018, Limaye 1990 abstract, Su 2018, Thomsen 2023, Kaushansky 2024, Hitchcock 2021, Feng 2015, Acha 2022). Pending, not taught: platelet lifespan and splenic pool, IL-3/kit ligand megakaryocyte support, giant platelets in MPN/MDS. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
